summary.text: Phytoplankton are the self-feeding part of the plankton: microscopic photosynthesizing bacteria and protists living in the sunlit upper layer of oceans and lakes.
Though they make up only about 1% of global plant biomass, they account for about half of global photosynthesis and at least half of oxygen production.
They form the base of marine and freshwater food webs, and besides light they depend on nutrients such as nitrate, phosphate and trace metals like iron.

paragraphs.heading: Plant drifters
paragraphs.text: Phytoplankton are the self-feeding members of the plankton and a key part of ocean and freshwater ecosystems. Their name joins Greek words for "plant" and "drifter". They are microscopic bacteria and protists that photosynthesize, living in the sunlit top layer of seas and lakes. Most are too small to see one by one, but in large numbers some show up as colored patches on the water, thanks to chlorophyll and, in some species, other pigments.

paragraphs.heading: Who counts
paragraphs.text: The group is very diverse, from cyanobacteria, which are photosynthesizing bacteria, to several kinds of single-celled protists, notably diatoms. Coccolithophores and dinoflagellates used to be counted as phytoplankton, but because they can also eat other organisms they are now called mixoplankton. A few species have no pigment at all and feed on other organisms or debris, such as the dinoflagellates Noctiluca and Dinophysis; these are often viewed as zooplankton.

paragraphs.heading: Living on light
paragraphs.text: Like trees and other land plants, phytoplankton get their energy from photosynthesis, so they must live in the well-lit surface layer called the euphotic zone. They take in carbon dioxide dissolved in the water, build organic compounds from it and release oxygen. Their many different pigments let different species capture different wavelengths of underwater light. Researchers found that changing only the mix of wavelengths, at the same brightness, can reshape natural communities. Too much sunlight can harm them through photodegradation.

paragraphs.heading: Small mass, huge output
paragraphs.text: Phytoplankton make up only about 1% of all plant biomass, yet they account for about half of global photosynthesis and at least half of oxygen production. The energy they lock into carbon compounds, called primary production, is the base of most ocean food webs and many freshwater ones, and they are key players in the carbon cycle. They are eaten by zooplankton, fish larvae and other consumers, and can also be broken down by bacteria or destroyed by viruses. Because they cannot move against currents, they slowly sink, and their dead cells and debris end up fertilizing the seafloor.

paragraphs.heading: Fast responders
paragraphs.text: Compared with land plants, phytoplankton cover a larger area, face less change with the seasons, and turn over far faster, in days rather than decades. As a result, they react quickly, across the whole globe, to shifts in climate.

paragraphs.heading: Nutrients and iron
paragraphs.text: Besides light, phytoplankton need nutrients, which reach the ocean from rivers, continental weathering and meltwater from polar ice. The main ones are nitrate, phosphate and silicic acid, needed in fairly large amounts. They also need trace metals such as iron, manganese, zinc and copper, and across big areas like the Southern Ocean a shortage of iron often holds them back. Some scientists have proposed adding iron to the sea to boost growth and draw carbon dioxide out of the air. Large experiments have tried it, but disputes over meddling with ecosystems and over how well it works have slowed them.
